topics.name: Evolutionary Biology
concepts: Oparin–Haldane: chemical evolution in a reducing atmosphere (CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O) without free O₂; Oparin's coacervates, Haldane's 'hot dilute soup'
Miller–Urey (1953): electric discharge through CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour gave simple amino acids (glycine, alanine)
First living forms were anaerobic heterotrophs (prokaryotes)
Homologous organs (same origin, different function) → divergent evolution; analogous organs (same function) → convergent evolution
Vestigial organs in man: vermiform appendix, nictitating membrane, coccyx, wisdom teeth, ear muscles; atavism = reappearance of ancestral traits (tail, extra nipples)
Connecting links: Archaeopteryx (reptiles–birds), Platypus (reptiles–mammals), Peripatus (Annelida–Arthropoda)
Horse evolution: Eohippus → Mesohippus → Merychippus → Pliohippus → Equus (paleontological evidence)
Haeckel's biogenetic law: ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny; gill pouches in all vertebrate embryos
Biochemical evidence: Nuttall's precipitin test shows man's serum closest to apes (chimpanzee)
Lamarck: use and disuse, inheritance of acquired characters (giraffe); disproved by Weismann (tails of mice)
Darwin: overproduction, struggle for existence (from Malthus), variation, natural selection; 'survival of the fittest' coined by Herbert Spencer
Neo-Darwinism: mutation, recombination, natural selection, reproductive isolation, genetic drift (Sewall Wright effect)
Hardy–Weinberg: p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1; carriers = 2pq
Human line: Ramapithecus (fossil at Tinau river, Butwal, Nepal) → Australopithecus → Homo habilis (tool maker) → H. erectus (fire) → H. sapiens

topics.name: Animal Diversity and Classification
concepts: Protozoa are classified by locomotory organelles: Sarcodina (pseudopodia), Mastigophora (flagella), Ciliata (cilia), Sporozoa (none) [repeat]
Porifera: ostia in, osculum out; choanocytes; spicules/spongin; archaeocytes are totipotent
Cnidaria: diploblastic, cnidoblasts (stinging cells); Obelia shows metagenesis; corals build reefs
Ctenophora: comb plates for swimming
Platyhelminthes: first triploblastic, bilateral, acoelomate; flame cells for excretion [repeat]
Aschelminthes: pseudocoelom; Ascaris male smaller with curved tail and penial spicules; hookworm larvae enter through bare feet [repeat]
Annelida: true metameric segmentation, schizocoelom, nephridia; leech secretes anticoagulant hirudin
Arthropoda: jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton, haemocoel, open circulation, Malpighian tubules (insects)
Mollusca: mantle, shell, radula; organ of Bojanus = kidney (Pila) [repeat]
Echinodermata: water vascular system, tube feet; larvae bilateral, adults pentaradial; Aristotle's lantern in sea urchin
Hemichordata Balanoglossus; Urochordata Herdmania (retrogressive metamorphosis); Cephalochordata Amphioxus
Cyclostomata jawless; Chondrichthyes placoid scales, no operculum; Osteichthyes operculum, swim bladder
Aves: pneumatic bones, no teeth; Mammalia: hair, mammary glands, diaphragm; platypus lays eggs, kangaroo has a pouch [repeat]

topics.name: Animal Tissues and Histology
concepts: Epithelium covers and protects; skin epidermis = stratified squamous keratinised [repeat]
Simple squamous: alveoli, blood vessels, Bowman's capsule; simple cuboidal: PCT, thyroid follicles, gland ducts
Simple columnar with microvilli: intestine; pseudostratified ciliated columnar: trachea; transitional: urinary bladder
Goblet cells secrete mucus; sebaceous glands holocrine, mammary apocrine, salivary/sweat merocrine
Junctions: tight (seal), adhering/desmosome (hold), gap (communication)
Areolar tissue: fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells (heparin, histamine); brown fat produces heat
Tendon: muscle to bone; ligament: bone to bone; collagen = white fibres, elastin = yellow fibres
Cartilage: hyaline (tracheal rings), elastic (pinna, epiglottis), fibrocartilage (intervertebral discs)
Compact bone: Haversian systems, osteocytes in lacunae, Volkmann's canals; protein ossein; blood is fluid connective tissue
Skeletal: striated, voluntary, multinucleate; smooth: unstriated, involuntary, spindle; cardiac: striated, involuntary, branched, intercalated discs
Red muscle fibres: myoglobin, many mitochondria, slow sustained work
Neuron: Nissl granules in cyton and dendrites, absent in axon; nodes of Ranvier allow saltatory conduction
Neuroglia: Schwann cells (PNS myelin), oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin), microglia (phagocytic); bipolar neurons in retina
Purkinje cells are neurons of the cerebellum; Purkinje fibres are cardiac conducting fibres

topics.name: Study of Selected Animals
concepts: Plasmodium: man = intermediate host (asexual schizogony), female Anopheles = definitive host (sexual phase, sporogony) [repeat]
Sporozoites → liver cells (pre-erythrocytic) → RBC cycle (ring stage, schizont) → merozoites; gametocytes form in human RBCs
Fever follows RBC rupture releasing merozoites and haemozoin; vivax 48 h (benign tertian), falciparum malignant tertian, malariae 72 h (quartan)
In mosquito: exflagellation, fertilisation in stomach → motile ookinete → oocyst on outer stomach wall → sporozoites in salivary glands
Laveran saw the parasite in human blood (1880); Ronald Ross proved mosquito transmission; hypnozoites cause vivax relapse; Schüffner's dots in vivax
Pheretima: ~100–120 segments; clitellum 14–16; female pore 14th; male pores 18th; 4 pairs spermathecal pores 5/6–8/9
Earthworm gut: gizzard 8–9, typhlosole from 26th segment; haemoglobin dissolved in plasma; 4 pairs of hearts (7, 9, 12, 13)
Earthworm nephridia: septal and pharyngeal open into gut (enteronephric); integumentary open on skin (exonephric) [repeat]
Earthworm: cutaneous respiration, protandrous hermaphrodite, cocoon, direct development; vermicomposting
Frog heart: sinus venosus, 2 auricles, 1 ventricle, truncus arteriosus; sinus venosus is pacemaker [repeat]
Frog respiration: cutaneous (sole route in hibernation), buccopharyngeal, pulmonary by buccal force pump; tadpole uses gills [repeat]
Male frog: vocal sacs (loud croak) and nuptial pads on first finger [repeat]
Frog: 9 vertebrae + urostyle, no ribs; columella auris; teeth only on upper jaw; tongue bifid and free behind
Frog: renal portal system, nucleated oval RBCs, 10 pairs of cranial nerves; male ureter is urinogenital duct; thyroxine drives metamorphosis

topics.name: Biota, Environment and Conservation
concepts: Reflex action is controlled by the spinal cord; taxis = directional movement towards/away from a stimulus (phototaxis)
Anadromous fish (salmon) swim from sea to river to spawn; catadromous (eel) from river to sea
High BOD = heavy organic pollution; eutrophication = N and P enrichment → algal bloom
DDT biomagnifies up the food chain, highest in top carnivores (fish-eating birds, thin eggshells)
Minamata disease = mercury; acid rain from SO₂ and NOₓ; CFCs deplete ozone
Volant adaptations: pneumatic bones, keeled sternum (birds); patagium (bats)
Desert adaptation: kangaroo rat survives on metabolic water; aquatic: streamlined body, fins, lateral line
Digitigrade = walking on toes (cat, dog); plantigrade = whole sole (man, bear); unguligrade = hooves (horse) [repeat]
Ramsar Convention (1971) protects wetlands; Koshi Tappu (1987) was Nepal's first Ramsar site
Biodiversity hotspot concept by Norman Myers; IUCN publishes the Red Data Book (CR, EN, VU categories)
Nepal: one-horned rhino (Chitwan), wild water buffalo/arna (Koshi Tappu), blackbuck (Khairapur, Bardiya), gharial critically endangered
In-situ: national parks, reserves, conservation areas; ex-situ: zoos, breeding centres, gene banks

questions.q: Which gas was NOT part of the mixture in the Miller–Urey spark-discharge experiment?
questions.x: The mixture copied a reducing primitive atmosphere: CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour. Free O₂ was absent; it would have oxidised the organic molecules formed.

questions.q: Which pair shows homologous organs?
o: Wing of bat and wing of butterfly
Forelimb of whale and wing of bat
Eye of octopus and eye of man
Wing of bird and wing of housefly
questions.x: Homologous organs share the same basic plan and origin (pentadactyl limb) but do different jobs — evidence of divergent evolution.
questions.trap: Bat and butterfly wings do the same job but have different origins: analogous.

questions.q: Lamarck's theory of evolution is known as
questions.x: Lamarck (1809) proposed use and disuse of organs and inheritance of acquired characters, e.g., the giraffe's long neck. Natural selection is Darwin's theory.

questions.q: Hugo de Vries proposed the mutation theory after studying
questions.x: De Vries saw sudden, heritable new forms in evening primrose (Oenothera lamarckiana) and called such discontinuous changes mutations.
questions.trap: Pisum sativum is Mendel's garden pea.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show a recessive trait. What is the frequency of heterozygotes?
questions.x: q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6. Heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48.
questions.trap: 0.24 forgets the 2 in 2pq; 0.36 is p² (homozygous dominant).

questions.q: The stage of Plasmodium that a mosquito injects into human blood is the
questions.x: Sporozoites from the mosquito's salivary glands enter human blood and first invade liver cells (pre-erythrocytic cycle).
questions.trap: Merozoites infect RBCs but are formed inside the human, not injected.

questions.q: The definitive host of Plasmodium vivax is
questions.x: Gametes of Plasmodium fuse (sexual reproduction) inside the female Anopheles, so it is the definitive host; humans are the intermediate host.
questions.trap: Humans show the disease, but only asexual cycles occur in them.

questions.q: In malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax, chills and fever recur every 48 hours because
o: sporozoites enter liver cells every 48 hours
infected RBCs burst every 48 hours releasing merozoites and toxins (haemozoin)
questions.x: The erythrocytic (Golgi) cycle of P. vivax takes 48 hours; synchronous rupture of RBCs releases merozoites and toxic haemozoin, causing fever — benign tertian malaria.

questions.q: The infective stage of Entamoeba histolytica for humans is the
questions.x: Mature quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated food or water are swallowed and excyst in the intestine. Trophozoites outside the body die and are killed by stomach acid.
questions.trap: The trophozoite causes the disease but cannot survive outside the host.

questions.q: During conjugation in Paramecium, the two partners exchange their
questions.x: The micronucleus divides meiotically; the surviving nucleus forms a stationary and a migratory pronucleus. Migratory pronuclei are exchanged and fuse with stationary ones; macronuclei degenerate.
questions.trap: Macronuclei disintegrate during conjugation; they are not exchanged.

questions.q: Choanocytes (collar cells) lining the canal system are characteristic of
questions.x: Sponges such as Sycon have flagellated collar cells that drive water through ostia and canals and trap food particles.

questions.q: Alternation of an asexual polyp generation with a sexual medusa generation (metagenesis) is seen in
questions.x: Obelia polyps bud off medusae asexually; medusae produce gametes, the zygote forms a planula larva that grows into a new polyp colony.
questions.trap: Hydra is a cnidarian but has only the polyp form.

questions.q: Man gets the intestinal tapeworm Taenia solium by eating undercooked pork containing
questions.x: Pigs swallow eggs; onchospheres become cysticerci in pig muscle (measly pork). Eating it undercooked releases the cysticercus, which grows into the adult worm in the human intestine.
questions.trap: Swallowing eggs causes cysticercosis, not the intestinal tapeworm.

questions.q: The correct sequence of larval stages in the life cycle of Fasciola hepatica is
questions.x: Miracidium enters the snail (Lymnaea) and becomes a sporocyst, then rediae, then cercariae; cercariae encyst on grass as metacercariae, which infect sheep.

questions.q: Ascaris lumbricoides has a body cavity that is a
questions.x: Aschelminthes have a pseudocoel: a cavity between body wall and gut not fully lined by mesoderm (a persistent blastocoel).

questions.q: The rasping, tongue-like radula used for feeding is found in
questions.x: The radula, a ribbon with chitinous teeth in the buccal cavity, is characteristic of molluscs such as Pila.

questions.q: A water vascular (ambulacral) system with tube feet is characteristic of
questions.x: Echinoderms such as Asterias (starfish) use the water vascular system for locomotion, food capture and respiration.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental character of chordates?
questions.x: All chordates show a notochord, dorsal tubular nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits at some stage. A ventral solid nerve cord belongs to non-chordates like earthworm and cockroach.

questions.q: Among reptiles, a completely four-chambered heart is found in
questions.x: Most reptiles have an incompletely divided ventricle; crocodiles have a complete interventricular septum, so the heart has four chambers.

questions.q: In Pheretima posthuma (earthworm), the clitellum covers segments
questions.x: The clitellum, a glandular girdle on segments 14–16, secretes the cocoon. The female pore is on segment 14 and paired male pores on 18.
questions.trap: Segment 18 carries the male genital pores, not the clitellum.

questions.q: The typhlosole in the intestine of the earthworm
questions.x: The typhlosole is a median dorsal fold of the intestinal wall projecting into the lumen; it increases the area for absorption of digested food.
questions.trap: Grinding is done by the gizzard, not the typhlosole.

questions.q: The excretory organs of the cockroach are
questions.x: Malpighian tubules at the junction of midgut and hindgut remove nitrogenous wastes and pass uric acid into the gut; the cockroach is uricotelic.
questions.trap: Nephridia are excretory organs of earthworm.

questions.q: The heart of the cockroach is a dorsal tube made of
questions.x: The cockroach heart is a 13-chambered tube with paired ostia; haemolymph flows in an open system through the haemocoel.

questions.q: The heart of an adult frog consists of
questions.x: The frog heart is three-chambered (two auricles, one ventricle) with an accessory sinus venosus dorsally and truncus arteriosus ventrally.

questions.q: With respect to nitrogenous waste, the tadpole and the adult frog are respectively
questions.x: The aquatic tadpole excretes ammonia, easily diluted in water; during metamorphosis the urea cycle develops and the adult frog excretes mainly urea.
questions.trap: Reversing the order: the tadpole, not the adult, is ammonotelic.

questions.q: The walls of the lung alveoli are lined by
questions.x: Thin, flat simple squamous cells allow rapid diffusion of gases; they also line blood vessels and Bowman's capsule.
questions.trap: Ciliated epithelium lines the trachea and bronchi, not alveoli.

questions.q: Intercalated discs are a feature of
questions.x: Intercalated discs join branched cardiac fibres; their gap junctions let impulses spread quickly so the heart contracts as one unit.

questions.q: Haversian canals surrounded by concentric lamellae are characteristic of
questions.x: Mammalian compact bone is organised into Haversian systems: a central canal with vessels and nerves, surrounded by lamellae with osteocytes in lacunae.

questions.q: The myelin sheath around peripheral nerve fibres is formed by
questions.x: In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells wrap around axons to form myelin; the gaps between them are nodes of Ranvier.
questions.trap: Oligodendrocytes form myelin in the CNS, not in peripheral nerves.

questions.q: The one-horned rhinoceros in Nepal is mainly conserved in
questions.x: Chitwan National Park (1973, a World Heritage Site) holds most of Nepal's one-horned rhinos; smaller populations live in Bardiya and Shuklaphanta.

questions.q: In a honeybee colony, drones develop from
o: fertilised eggs fed royal jelly throughout
fertilised eggs fed royal jelly only for the first few days
questions.x: Drones (males) are haploid and develop from unfertilised eggs. Fertilised eggs give females: queens if fed royal jelly throughout, workers otherwise.
questions.trap: Royal jelly throughout produces a queen, not a drone.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of ex-situ conservation?
questions.x: Ex-situ conservation protects species outside their natural habitat: zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks. Parks and reserves are in-situ.

questions.q: According to Oparin and Haldane, the primitive atmosphere of the earth was
o: Mainly nitrogen and oxygen, as today
questions.x: Oparin–Haldane proposed a reducing atmosphere of CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour. With no free O₂, organic molecules formed by chemical evolution were not destroyed by oxidation.

questions.q: Colloidal droplets called coacervates, thought to be forerunners of the first cells, were proposed by
questions.x: Oparin suggested that organic molecules in the primitive sea aggregated into coacervates. Fox made proteinoid microspheres; Haldane described the sea as a hot dilute soup.
questions.trap: Sidney Fox is picked, but he made microspheres, not coacervates.

questions.q: In the Miller–Urey apparatus, the energy for the chemical reactions was supplied mainly by
questions.x: Miller passed electric sparks (copying lightning) through CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour; boiling water only circulated the vapour.

questions.q: The Miller–Urey experiment produced
o: Simple amino acids such as glycine and alanine
questions.x: After a week of sparking, the condensed liquid contained simple organic compounds, mainly amino acids like glycine and alanine. No nucleic acids or cells formed.

questions.q: The first living organisms on earth are believed to have been
questions.x: The early atmosphere had no free O₂, and the sea was full of ready-made organic food, so the first prokaryotes were anaerobic heterotrophs. Photosynthesis and O₂ came later.

questions.q: The wings of a butterfly and the wings of a bird are
questions.x: They do the same job (flight) but have different origin and structure: insect wings are cuticle outgrowths, bird wings are modified forelimbs.
questions.trap: Same function tempts 'homologous'; homology means same origin.

questions.q: Analogous organs provide evidence for
questions.x: Unrelated groups facing similar demands evolve similar-looking structures independently: convergent evolution. Homologous organs show divergent evolution.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vestigial organ in humans?
o: Nictitating membrane (plica semilunaris) of the eye
questions.x: The plica semilunaris is a functionless remnant of the third eyelid seen in frogs and birds. Pancreas, patella and epiglottis all work.

questions.q: The sudden appearance of a short tail or extra nipples in a human baby is an example of
questions.x: Atavism (reversion) is the reappearance of an ancestral character that is normally absent. It shows that the genes still exist from our ancestors.
questions.trap: Vestigial organs are present in everyone and reduced; atavistic traits appear only occasionally.

questions.q: The fossil Archaeopteryx is a connecting link between
questions.x: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings (bird) but also teeth, a long bony tail and clawed fingers (reptile).

questions.q: Peripatus is a living connecting link between
questions.x: Peripatus has annelid features (segmental nephridia, unjointed legs, soft body) and arthropod features (tracheae, haemocoel, claws).

questions.q: The duck-billed platypus is regarded as a connecting link between
questions.x: Platypus lays eggs and has a cloaca like reptiles, yet has hair and mammary glands like mammals.
questions.trap: The duck-like bill tempts 'birds', but egg-laying and cloaca are reptilian features.

questions.q: The earliest known ancestor in the evolution of the horse is
questions.x: Fossil sequence: Eohippus (dawn horse, 4 toes in front) → Mesohippus → Merychippus → Pliohippus → Equus (single hoof). It is classic paleontological evidence.

questions.q: 'Ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny' (biogenetic law) was stated by
questions.x: Haeckel's recapitulation theory says an embryo passes through stages resembling its ancestors. Von Baer only noted that embryos of related animals look alike.
questions.trap: Von Baer studied embryo similarity, but the recapitulation law is Haeckel's.

questions.q: The presence of pharyngeal gill pouches in the human embryo is
questions.x: All vertebrate embryos, including man, develop gill pouches, showing descent from a common aquatic ancestor. Evidence from embryos is embryological.

questions.q: Nuttall's precipitin test on blood serum showed that human serum proteins are most similar to those of the
questions.x: The stronger the precipitate formed with anti-human serum, the closer the relationship. Apes such as the chimpanzee gave the strongest reaction: biochemical evidence.

questions.q: Who cut off the tails of mice over many generations and showed that tail-less young never appeared?
questions.x: Weismann's experiment disproved inheritance of acquired characters (Lamarckism). He proposed the germplasm theory: only germ-cell changes are inherited.

questions.q: The phrase 'survival of the fittest' was coined by
questions.x: Herbert Spencer coined the phrase after reading Darwin; Darwin later used it as an equivalent of natural selection.
questions.trap: Darwin is chosen because the idea is his, but the phrase is Spencer's.

questions.q: Darwin's idea of 'struggle for existence' was inspired by
questions.x: Malthus argued that populations grow faster than food supply, so many must die. Darwin applied this to all organisms. Mendel and de Vries were unknown to him.

questions.q: Darwin's observations of finches with different beaks were made on the
questions.x: During the voyage of HMS Beagle, Darwin saw many finch species on the Galapagos, each with a beak suited to its food: adaptive radiation from a common ancestor.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor of the modern synthetic theory (Neo-Darwinism)?
questions.x: Neo-Darwinism combines mutation, recombination, natural selection, genetic drift and reproductive isolation. Inheritance of acquired characters is Lamarck's idea and is rejected.

questions.q: The Sewall Wright effect refers to
questions.x: Sewall Wright showed that allele frequencies change by chance in small populations: random genetic drift.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the recessive allele is 0.3. The frequency of homozygous dominant individuals is
questions.x: q = 0.3, so p = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7; homozygous dominant = p² = 0.7² = 0.49.
questions.trap: 0.42 is 2pq, the heterozygotes.

questions.q: In a Hardy–Weinberg population, 1 in 100 individuals shows a recessive disorder. The frequency of carriers (heterozygotes) is
questions.trap: 0.01 is q², the affected individuals, not carriers.

questions.q: In Nepal, a fossil of Ramapithecus was discovered near
questions.x: A Ramapithecus jaw/teeth fossil was found in the Siwalik deposits of Tinau river near Butwal. Ramapithecus is considered an early hominid-like ape.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: The first human species known to make stone tools ('handy man') is
questions.x: Homo habilis made simple stone tools. Homo erectus was first to use fire; Australopithecus was an upright ape-man with no regular tool-making.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: Java man and Peking man belong to the species
questions.x: Java man (Pithecanthropus) and Peking man (Sinanthropus) are both Homo erectus, which walked fully erect and used fire.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: Which prehistoric man made cave paintings and is regarded as the direct ancestor of modern man?
questions.x: Cro-Magnon man was an early Homo sapiens sapiens with modern skull, fine tools and cave art. Neanderthals buried their dead but are a side branch.
questions.trap: Neanderthal man is famous, but he is not our direct ancestor.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: The correct sequence in human evolution is
o: Australopithecus → Ramapithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
Ramapithecus → Homo habilis → Australopithecus → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
Ramapithecus → Australopithecus → Homo erectus → Homo habilis → Homo sapiens
Ramapithecus → Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
questions.x: Ramapithecus (ape-like) → Australopithecus (upright ape-man) → Homo habilis (tool maker) → Homo erectus (fire) → Homo sapiens.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: The 'southern ape', the first ape-man that walked upright on two legs, is
questions.x: Australopithecus fossils (e.g. Taung child) from southern Africa show bipedal walking with an ape-sized brain.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: According to Hugo de Vries, new species arise by
questions.x: De Vries (Oenothera) held that evolution is discontinuous: mutations appear suddenly and can form a new species in one step (saltation).

questions.q: Industrial melanism in the peppered moth (Biston betularia) is an example of
questions.x: Soot darkened tree trunks, so birds ate the conspicuous light moths and the dark form increased. The environment selected the better-camouflaged variety.

questions.q: Protozoa are mainly classified on the basis of their
questions.x: Classes: Sarcodina (pseudopodia), Mastigophora (flagella), Ciliata (cilia) and Sporozoa (no locomotory organelles).

questions.q: Which class of Protozoa has no locomotory organelles in the adult stage?
questions.x: Sporozoa such as Plasmodium are all parasites and lack pseudopodia, flagella and cilia in the adult; they spread by spores (sporozoites).

questions.q: Under the classification of Protozoa, Euglena is placed in
questions.x: Euglena moves by a long flagellum, so it is a flagellate (Mastigophora).

questions.q: Kala-azar is caused by ____ and spread by ____.
questions.x: Leishmania donovani, a flagellate protozoan, causes kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) and is carried by the sand fly. Trypanosoma and tsetse fly cause sleeping sickness.

questions.q: In a sponge, water leaves the body through the
questions.x: Water enters through many small ostia, passes the spongocoel lined by choanocytes, and leaves through the large osculum.

questions.q: The totipotent cells of sponges that can form any other cell type are
questions.x: Archaeocytes are amoeboid, undifferentiated cells that form gametes, gemmules and other cells and help in regeneration.

questions.q: Stinging cells (cnidoblasts) with nematocysts are characteristic of
questions.x: Cnidoblasts discharge nematocysts for offence and defence, e.g. in Hydra, Obelia and jellyfish; the phylum is named after them.

questions.q: Animals that swim using eight rows of ciliary comb plates belong to
questions.x: Ctenophores (comb jellies, e.g. Pleurobrachia) have 8 rows of comb plates and lack cnidoblasts.

questions.q: Flame cells are the excretory structures of
questions.x: Flame cells (protonephridia) of flatworms like Planaria and Fasciola remove wastes; the beating cilia look like a flickering flame.

questions.q: The first animals to show bilateral symmetry with three germ layers but no body cavity are
questions.x: Flatworms are the first triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical animals and are acoelomate. Cnidaria are diploblastic; Aschelminthes have a pseudocoelom.

questions.q: A male Ascaris differs from the female in having
o: A curved posterior end with penial spicules
questions.x: Ascaris shows sexual dimorphism: the male is smaller with a ventrally curved tail bearing penial spicules; the female is longer with a straight tail.

questions.q: Walking barefoot on soil contaminated with human faeces is the usual way of getting infected by
questions.x: Hookworm filariform larvae in soil penetrate the skin of bare feet. Ascaris and Enterobius are swallowed as eggs; Taenia comes from measly pork.

questions.q: True metameric segmentation first appears in
questions.x: Annelids (earthworm, leech, Nereis) have a body divided internally and externally into similar segments separated by septa.

questions.q: The anticoagulant hirudin is secreted by
questions.x: Salivary glands of the leech (Hirudinaria) secrete hirudin, which stops the host's blood from clotting while it feeds.

questions.q: The body cavity of arthropods is a
questions.x: In arthropods the coelom is reduced and the main cavity is filled with blood (haemolymph) from an open circulatory system: haemocoel.

questions.q: The organ of Bojanus, which works as a kidney, is found in
questions.x: The organ of Bojanus is the excretory organ (kidney) of molluscs such as Pila and Unio.

questions.q: Which of the following is a true fish?
questions.x: Seahorse is a bony fish with gills and fins. Cuttlefish is a mollusc, silverfish an insect, jellyfish a cnidarian.
questions.trap: Names ending in 'fish' mislead; check the phylum.

questions.q: Aristotle's lantern, a chewing apparatus, is found in
questions.x: Sea urchins (Echinus) have a five-jawed chewing apparatus called Aristotle's lantern.

questions.q: Which statement about echinoderms is correct?
o: They live in fresh water as well as the sea
Their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical but adults are pentaradial
questions.x: Echinoderms are exclusively marine, coelomate (enterocoelous) animals with a calcareous endoskeleton. Bilateral larvae show their descent from bilateral ancestors.

questions.q: Balanoglossus (tongue worm) belongs to
questions.x: Balanoglossus has a proboscis, collar and trunk, with a stomochord in the proboscis; it is placed in Hemichordata.

questions.q: Retrogressive metamorphosis, in which a free-swimming larva with a notochord changes into a sessile adult without it, occurs in
questions.x: In urochordates like Herdmania the notochord is only in the larval tail; during metamorphosis the larva loses tail, notochord and nerve cord.

questions.q: In which animal does the notochord extend from the head to the tail throughout life?
questions.x: Cephalochordates like Amphioxus keep the notochord along the whole body, even beyond the nerve cord at the front. Vertebrates replace it with a vertebral column.

questions.q: Jawless vertebrates such as lamprey (Petromyzon) and hagfish (Myxine) belong to
questions.x: Cyclostomes have a circular sucking mouth without jaws, no paired fins and a cartilaginous skeleton.

questions.q: Placoid scales are found in
questions.x: Cartilaginous fishes have tooth-like placoid scales. Bony fishes like rohu have cycloid/ctenoid scales; frogs have no scales.

questions.q: A bony operculum covering the gills and an air (swim) bladder are present in
questions.x: These are features of bony fishes (Osteichthyes). Scoliodon and Torpedo are cartilaginous fishes with naked gill slits and no air bladder.

questions.q: Pneumatic (air-filled) bones are a characteristic of
questions.x: Hollow bones connected to air sacs make birds light for flight.

questions.q: A muscular diaphragm separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities is found only in
questions.x: The diaphragm is a diagnostic mammalian feature and helps in breathing.

questions.q: Which of the following mammals lays eggs?
questions.x: Platypus and spiny anteater (Prototheria) are oviparous mammals. Kangaroo, bat and whale give birth to young (viviparous).

questions.q: A pouch (marsupium) in which the young complete development is found in
questions.x: Kangaroo is a marsupial (Metatheria): the tiny young crawls into the mother's pouch and feeds on milk there.

questions.q: The tissue that covers body surfaces and lines body cavities, mainly for protection, is
questions.x: Epithelium forms the outer skin and lines cavities and tubes; it protects, absorbs and secretes. It rests on a basement membrane and has no blood vessels.

questions.q: The epidermis of human skin is made of
questions.x: Many layers of flat cells with dead keratin-filled outer cells resist friction, water loss and germs: the main protective epithelium.

questions.q: The proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron is lined by
o: Simple cuboidal epithelium with brush border
questions.x: PCT cells are cube-shaped with microvilli (brush border) for reabsorption. Bowman's capsule is simple squamous.

questions.q: The inner lining of the trachea is
questions.x: One layer of columnar cells of different heights looks layered; cilia and goblet-cell mucus trap and sweep out dust.

questions.q: The stretchable epithelium lining the urinary bladder is
questions.x: Transitional epithelium changes from many rounded layers to fewer flattened layers when the bladder fills.

questions.q: The inner lining of the small intestine is
questions.x: Tall columnar cells with microvilli (brush border) increase surface area for absorption; goblet cells among them secrete mucus.

questions.q: Goblet cells are unicellular glands that secrete
questions.x: Goblet cells in intestinal and respiratory epithelium secrete mucus for lubrication and protection.

questions.q: Junctions that allow ions and small molecules to pass directly between neighbouring cells are
questions.x: Gap junctions are protein channels joining the cytoplasm of adjacent cells. Tight junctions seal gaps; desmosomes hold cells together.

questions.q: Sebaceous glands, in which the whole cell breaks down to form the secretion, are
questions.x: In holocrine glands the cells fill with secretion and rupture. Mammary glands are apocrine (tip lost); salivary and eccrine sweat glands are merocrine.
questions.trap: Mammary glands are apocrine; do not mix the two skin-gland types.

questions.q: In areolar connective tissue, heparin and histamine are secreted by
questions.x: Mast cells release heparin (anticoagulant) and histamine (vasodilation, allergy). Fibroblasts make fibres; macrophages engulf microbes.

questions.q: Brown adipose tissue, abundant in newborns and hibernating animals, is specialised for
questions.x: Brown fat cells have many mitochondria that release energy as heat (non-shivering thermogenesis) instead of making ATP.

questions.q: Choose the correct pair.
o: Tendon – bone to bone; ligament – muscle to bone
Tendon – muscle to bone; ligament – bone to bone
Tendon – muscle to muscle; ligament – bone to muscle
Tendon – skin to muscle; ligament – muscle to bone
questions.x: Tendons (dense white fibrous tissue) attach muscles to bones; ligaments (elastic fibrous tissue) join bones at joints.

questions.q: The pinna (external ear) is supported by
questions.x: Elastic cartilage has many yellow elastic fibres, so the pinna and epiglottis can bend and spring back.

questions.q: Intervertebral discs are made of
questions.x: White fibrocartilage, rich in collagen bundles, is tough and acts as a shock absorber between vertebrae and at the pubic symphysis.

questions.q: The C-shaped rings of the trachea are made of
questions.x: Hyaline cartilage, with a clear glassy matrix, keeps the trachea open; it also covers joint surfaces and forms the nose.

questions.q: In mammalian compact bone, the channels connecting Haversian canals with each other are
questions.x: Volkmann's canals run across the bone, linking Haversian canals and the periosteum. Canaliculi are tiny channels joining lacunae.

questions.q: The protein of the bone matrix is
questions.x: Bone matrix has ossein (a collagen protein) hardened by calcium phosphate salts. Chondrin is the cartilage matrix.
questions.trap: Chondrin is cartilage, not bone.

questions.q: Blood is classified as a
questions.x: Blood, like other connective tissues, arises from mesoderm and has cells in an extracellular matrix, here the liquid plasma.

questions.q: Muscle fibres that are striated, involuntary and branched are
questions.x: Cardiac fibres are striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary like smooth muscle, branched and joined by intercalated discs.

questions.q: The muscle found in the walls of the stomach, intestine and blood vessels is
questions.x: Spindle-shaped, uninucleate, unstriated, involuntary smooth muscle produces slow, sustained contractions such as peristalsis.

questions.q: Which muscle fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleate?
questions.x: Each skeletal fibre forms by fusion of many myoblasts, so it is a multinucleate syncytium with peripheral nuclei.

questions.q: Red muscle fibres differ from white fibres in having
o: Less myoglobin, for fast anaerobic bursts
More myoglobin and mitochondria, for slow sustained aerobic work
questions.x: Red fibres store O₂ on myoglobin and respire aerobically, so they resist fatigue (e.g. flight muscles of birds, postural muscles). White fibres work fast but tire quickly.

questions.q: Nissl's granules are absent from the
questions.x: Nissl's granules (rough ER with ribosomes) are found in the cyton and dendrites but not in the axon or axon hillock.

questions.q: Nerve impulses jump from one node of Ranvier to the next in
questions.x: Myelin insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier; this saltatory conduction is much faster.

questions.q: The neuroglial cells that act as phagocytes in the central nervous system are
questions.x: Microglia are small macrophage-like cells that engulf debris and microbes. Oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells make myelin; astrocytes support neurons.

questions.q: Bipolar neurons are found in the
questions.x: Bipolar neurons, with one dendrite and one axon, occur in the retina and olfactory epithelium. Motor neurons are multipolar; dorsal root ganglion cells are pseudo-unipolar.

questions.q: Purkinje cells, large neurons with richly branched dendrites, are found in the
questions.x: Purkinje cells are neurons of the cerebellar cortex. Purkinje fibres of the heart ventricles are modified cardiac muscle fibres.
questions.trap: Purkinje fibres (heart) are different from Purkinje cells (cerebellum).

questions.q: In the life cycle of Plasmodium, man acts as the
questions.x: Only asexual multiplication (schizogony) occurs in man, so man is the intermediate host. Sexual reproduction occurs in the female Anopheles, the definitive host.

questions.q: Malignant tertian malaria is caused by
questions.x: P. falciparum causes the most dangerous (malignant, cerebral) malaria; infected RBCs stick in brain capillaries. P. vivax causes benign tertian malaria.

questions.q: Quartan malaria, with fever every 72 hours, is caused by
questions.x: The erythrocytic cycle of P. malariae takes 72 hours, so fever recurs on the fourth day (quartan).

questions.q: Sporozoites injected by a mosquito first enter the human
questions.x: Sporozoites reach the liver within about half an hour and multiply there (pre-erythrocytic schizogony) before merozoites invade RBCs.
questions.trap: Students say RBCs, but the RBC stage comes only after the liver stage.

questions.q: Haemozoin in the malarial cycle is
o: An infective stage injected by the mosquito
A toxic pigment formed when the parasite digests haemoglobin
questions.x: The trophozoite digests haemoglobin and leaves haemozoin. It is released with merozoites when RBCs burst and contributes to the chill and fever.

questions.q: The early trophozoite of Plasmodium inside an RBC, with a large vacuole pushing the nucleus to one side, is the
questions.x: The young trophozoite looks like a signet ring: a ring of cytoplasm with a nucleus as the 'stone'. It grows into a schizont that divides into merozoites.

questions.q: Schüffner's dots are seen in red blood cells infected by
questions.x: Infected RBCs of P. vivax become enlarged and show red Schüffner's dots. Falciparum shows Maurer's clefts and malariae Ziemann's dots.

questions.q: The motile, worm-like zygote of Plasmodium formed in the mosquito's stomach is the
questions.x: After fertilisation in the mosquito's stomach, the zygote elongates into a motile ookinete that bores into the stomach wall and becomes an oocyst.

questions.q: In the mosquito, the oocyst of Plasmodium develops on the
questions.x: The ookinete crosses the stomach wall and rounds up as an oocyst under its outer membrane; sporozoites formed inside then travel to the salivary glands.

questions.q: Sporozoites of Plasmodium are stored in the mosquito's
questions.x: Sporozoites released from the oocyst move through the haemolymph to the salivary glands and are injected when the mosquito bites.

questions.q: The asexual multiplication of Plasmodium inside the oocyst in the mosquito is called
questions.x: In man asexual multiplication is schizogony (liver and RBC). In the mosquito, the oocyst nucleus divides repeatedly to form thousands of sporozoites: sporogony.

questions.q: The malarial parasite was first observed in human blood by
questions.x: Laveran saw Plasmodium in a malaria patient's blood in 1880. Ronald Ross later found its stages in the mosquito.
questions.trap: Ronald Ross is famous for malaria, but for mosquito transmission.

questions.q: Who proved that malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes?
questions.x: Ronald Ross (1897) found Plasmodium oocysts in the stomach of an Anopheles mosquito and won the Nobel Prize in 1902.

questions.q: Relapse of vivax malaria months after apparent cure is due to
o: Reinfection by the same mosquito only
questions.x: In P. vivax (and ovale) some sporozoites stay dormant in the liver as hypnozoites; later they wake, release merozoites and cause relapse.

questions.q: Gametocytes of Plasmodium are formed in
questions.x: Some merozoites in RBCs develop into male and female gametocytes. They mature only when a female Anopheles sucks them up.
questions.trap: Gametes form in the mosquito, but gametocytes form in man.

questions.q: Exflagellation, the formation of microgametes from the male gametocyte of Plasmodium, takes place in the
questions.x: The cooler temperature and conditions in the mosquito's stomach trigger the male gametocyte to throw out several flagella-like microgametes.

questions.q: In Pheretima, septal nephridia discharge their excretory fluid into the
questions.x: Septal nephridia (on septa behind the 15th segment) open into the intestine through septal excretory canals: they are enteronephric, which helps conserve water.

questions.q: Which nephridia of Pheretima open directly to the outside on the body surface (exonephric)?
questions.x: Tiny integumentary nephridia on the body wall open by nephridiopores on the skin. Septal and pharyngeal nephridia open into the gut (enteronephric).

questions.q: In Pheretima, the single female genital aperture lies on segment
questions.x: One median female pore is on the ventral side of the 14th segment, inside the clitellum. Male pores are on the 18th.

questions.q: The pair of male genital apertures of Pheretima is on segment
questions.x: One pair of male genital pores lies ventrolaterally on the 18th segment, each on a small papilla.

questions.q: Spermathecal openings of Pheretima are
o: Four pairs, in the grooves 5/6 to 8/9
A single opening on the 14th segment
questions.x: Four pairs of spermathecal pores lie ventrolaterally in the intersegmental grooves between segments 5/6, 6/7, 7/8 and 8/9.

questions.q: The muscular gizzard of Pheretima, which grinds soil and food, lies in segments
questions.x: The thick-walled gizzard lies behind the oesophagus in segments 8–9. Segments 14–16 form the clitellum; the intestine starts after the stomach.

questions.q: In Pheretima, the typhlosole begins in segment
questions.x: The typhlosole is a dorsal fold of the intestine from the 26th segment backwards; it increases absorptive area. Intestinal caeca also arise in segment 26.

questions.q: The respiratory pigment of earthworm is
questions.x: Earthworm blood is red because haemoglobin is dissolved in the plasma; its corpuscles are colourless.
questions.trap: Red blood suggests RBCs, but earthworm corpuscles are colourless.

questions.q: The hearts of Pheretima are
questions.x: Pheretima has 4 pairs of hearts: lateral hearts in 7 and 9 and lateral-oesophageal hearts in 12 and 13; they pump blood into the ventral vessel.

questions.q: In the dorsal blood vessel of the earthworm, blood flows
questions.x: The dorsal vessel has valves and pumps blood forward; the ventral vessel carries blood backwards. Circulation is closed.

questions.q: Gaseous exchange in the earthworm occurs through its
questions.x: Earthworms have no respiratory organs; O₂ dissolves in the mucus-moist skin and diffuses into the dense capillary network.

questions.q: Although the earthworm is hermaphrodite, cross-fertilisation occurs because it is
questions.x: In Pheretima the male organs mature first (protandry), so sperm of one worm must fertilise eggs of another.

questions.q: Testes of Pheretima are
questions.x: Two pairs of testes lie in testis sacs in segments 10 and 11; one pair of ovaries lies in segment 13.

questions.q: Development in the earthworm is
o: Direct, inside a cocoon, with no larval stage
questions.x: The clitellum secretes a cocoon in which fertilisation and direct development occur; young worms hatch without a larva.

questions.q: Using earthworms to convert organic waste into manure is called
questions.x: Earthworms eat organic matter and release nutrient-rich castings (vermicompost); they also loosen and aerate soil, so they are called friends of farmers.

questions.q: In Pheretima, setae are absent from
o: The first segment, last segment and clitellum
questions.x: S-shaped setae form a ring in each segment except the first, the last and the clitellar segments 14–16.

questions.q: The cerebral (suprapharyngeal) ganglia of Pheretima lie in segment
questions.x: A pair of cerebral ganglia lies dorsal to the pharynx in segment 3 and joins the subpharyngeal ganglia by a nerve ring.

questions.q: Which chamber acts as the pacemaker in the frog's heart?
questions.x: The frog heart has a dorsal sinus venosus where the heartbeat starts. In man it is absent as a chamber; its remnant forms the SA node in the right atrium.

questions.q: The loud croaking of the male frog is due to
questions.x: Male frogs have vocal sacs that act as resonators and amplify the croak during the breeding season. Females lack them.

questions.q: During hibernation, the frog respires only through its
questions.x: In hibernation the frog lies inactive in mud, so lung and buccal breathing stop; the moist, vascular skin alone exchanges gases (cutaneous respiration).

questions.q: Air is forced into the lungs of a frog by
o: Raising the floor of the buccal cavity with the nostrils closed
Movement of ribs and intercostal muscles
Contraction of muscles in the lung wall
questions.x: Frogs have no diaphragm and no ribs. They fill the mouth with air, close the nostrils and lift the buccal floor, pushing air into the lungs (positive pressure).

questions.q: A young tadpole respires mainly through its
questions.x: The aquatic tadpole first has external gills, then internal gills; lungs develop during metamorphosis.

questions.q: A frog takes in water mainly
questions.x: Frogs do not drink water; the permeable skin absorbs it.

questions.q: Nuptial (copulatory) pads that help the male frog hold the female in amplexus are on the
questions.x: In the breeding season the male develops a swollen pad on the first digit of each forelimb to grip the female.

questions.q: The single ear ossicle of the frog is
questions.x: Frogs have no external ear; the tympanum passes vibrations through one rod-like ossicle, the columella auris, to the inner ear. Mammals have three ossicles.

questions.q: Which statement about the frog's teeth is correct?
o: Teeth are present on both jaws
Teeth are absent on both jaws
Teeth are present on the upper jaw but absent on the lower jaw
Teeth are present only on the lower jaw
questions.x: Frogs have maxillary and vomerine teeth in the upper jaw only; they hold prey and do not chew.

questions.q: The frog's tongue is
o: Bifid, free in front and attached behind
Bifid, attached in front and free behind
questions.x: The sticky bilobed tongue is attached at the front of the lower jaw, so it can be flicked out to catch insects.

questions.q: In the male frog, the duct that carries both urine and sperm is the
questions.x: Sperm pass from testes through vasa efferentia into the kidney and then the ureter, so the male ureter is a urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca.

questions.q: Fat bodies attached to the gonads of the frog
questions.x: Yellow finger-like fat bodies store fat that is used up during hibernation and gamete formation.

questions.q: Which of the following is present in the frog but absent in man?
questions.x: In frogs, blood from the hind limbs passes through the kidneys via the renal portal vein. Mammals have no renal portal system; both have a hepatic portal system.

questions.q: The vertebral column of the frog consists of
o: 9 vertebrae and a urostyle, with no ribs
questions.x: A frog has 9 vertebrae followed by a rod-like urostyle; ribs are absent.

questions.q: Red blood cells of the frog are
questions.x: Frog RBCs are large, oval and nucleated. Mammalian RBCs are non-nucleated.

questions.q: Metamorphosis of a tadpole into a frog is controlled by
questions.x: Thyroxine from the thyroid triggers tail resorption, limb growth and lung development; without iodine/thyroxine, tadpoles fail to metamorphose. Ecdysone controls insect moulting.

questions.q: The number of pairs of cranial nerves in the frog is
questions.x: Frogs have 10 pairs of cranial nerves; man has 12. 31 pairs is the number of human spinal nerves.

questions.q: The winter sleep of the frog is called
questions.x: Frogs burrow into mud and become inactive in winter (hibernation); summer sleep is aestivation.

questions.q: In the frog, the pulmocutaneous arch supplies blood to the
questions.x: The truncus arteriosus gives three arches on each side: carotid (head), systemic (body) and pulmocutaneous (lungs and skin, where blood is oxygenated).

questions.q: Movement of Euglena towards light is an example of
questions.x: Taxis is directional movement of a whole motile organism in response to a stimulus; towards light is positive phototaxis.

questions.q: A simple reflex action such as the knee jerk is controlled by the
questions.x: In a reflex arc, the impulse passes from receptor to spinal cord to effector without needing the brain, so the response is quick and automatic.

questions.q: Fishes such as salmon that migrate from the sea to rivers to spawn are called
questions.x: Anadromous fishes (salmon, hilsa) breed in fresh water and live in the sea. Catadromous fishes (eel) do the reverse.

questions.q: A high BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) of a water sample indicates
questions.x: BOD is the O₂ microbes need to decompose organic matter. More sewage gives more microbial activity, higher BOD and less dissolved O₂ for fish.

questions.q: Through biomagnification, DDT reaches its highest concentration in
o: Fish-eating birds at the top of the food chain
questions.x: DDT is fat-soluble and not excreted, so its concentration increases at each trophic level; top carnivores like fish-eating birds get thin-shelled eggs.

questions.q: Excess nitrates and phosphates in a lake cause algal blooms. This is called
questions.x: Nutrient enrichment (from fertiliser runoff and sewage) causes algal blooms; their decay uses up oxygen and kills fish.

questions.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning with
questions.x: Methyl mercury from factory waste in Minamata Bay, Japan, accumulated in fish and damaged the nervous system of people who ate them. Cadmium causes itai-itai.

questions.q: Acid rain is mainly caused by
o: Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
questions.x: SO₂ and NOₓ from burning fossil fuels dissolve in rain to form H₂SO₄ and HNO₃.

questions.q: Depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer is mainly caused by
questions.x: UV light releases chlorine atoms from CFCs; each chlorine atom destroys many ozone molecules.
questions.trap: CO₂ causes global warming, not ozone depletion.

questions.q: The flight membrane of a bat, stretched between elongated fingers, body and hind limbs, is the
questions.x: Bats are the only true flying (volant) mammals; the skin fold called the patagium forms the wing.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an adaptation of birds for flight?
o: Heavy, solid bones filled with marrow
questions.x: Flight needs low weight and strong muscles: hollow air-filled bones, a keel for flight muscles and no urinary bladder all reduce weight.

questions.q: The desert kangaroo rat can live without drinking water because it
o: Uses metabolic water and excretes very concentrated urine
questions.x: It obtains water from oxidation of food (metabolic water), has long loops of Henle for concentrated urine and stays in burrows by day.

questions.q: The lateral line system of fishes helps them to
questions.x: Lateral line sense organs detect pressure changes and vibrations in water, helping in orientation and avoiding enemies.

questions.q: Animals such as cats and dogs that walk on their toes are called
questions.x: Digitigrade animals walk on their digits with the heel raised, which helps fast running. Man and bear are plantigrade; horse and deer (hoofs) are unguligrade.

questions.q: Nepal's first Ramsar site, listed in 1987, is
questions.x: Koshi Tappu became Nepal's first wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention in 1987.

questions.q: The Ramsar Convention (1971) is an international treaty for the conservation of
questions.x: Signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, it protects wetlands of international importance, especially as waterbird habitat.

questions.q: The concept of 'biodiversity hotspots' was introduced by
questions.x: Norman Myers (1988) defined hotspots as regions with very high endemism under severe threat. Nepal is part of the Himalaya hotspot.

questions.q: The Red Data Book of threatened species is published by
questions.x: The IUCN Red List classifies species as Extinct, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, etc.

questions.q: In the IUCN Red List, the gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is categorised as
questions.x: Gharial numbers are very low; Nepal breeds and releases them from the gharial breeding centre in Chitwan.
questions.s: Conservation biology: Endangered species of Nepal

questions.q: Koshi Tappu in Nepal was established mainly to protect the
questions.x: Koshi Tappu, on the Koshi floodplain, protects the last population of wild water buffalo (arna) in Nepal and many waterbirds.

questions.q: The blackbuck in Nepal is conserved at
questions.x: The Blackbuck Conservation Area at Khairapur, Bardiya protects Nepal's only population of blackbuck (krishnasar).
questions.s: Conservation biology: Endangered species of Nepal

questions.q: Which feature is found in modern man but NOT in apes?
questions.x: A chin, large brain (about 1350 cc), S-shaped spine and habitual upright walking mark modern man. Apes also have opposable thumbs, menstrual cycles and no tail.
questions.s: Human evolution: From Ramapithecus to modern man

questions.q: According to Darwin, complex organs develop over many generations mainly through
o: Use and disuse of organs during an animal's life
Inheritance of characters acquired during life
Direct action of the environment creating needed organs
Natural selection of small favourable variations among overproduced offspring
questions.x: Darwin: overproduction → struggle for existence → variations → survival of the fittest → natural selection. Use and disuse and inheritance of acquired characters are Lamarck's ideas.
questions.trap: Use and disuse is Lamarckism, not Darwinism.

questions.q: Amphids, a pair of small pits on the lips of Ascaris, are
questions.x: Amphids on the lateral lips sense chemicals; phasmids near the tail are also chemosensory. Spicules are male copulatory organs.

questions.q: The correct order of canal systems in sponges, from simplest to most complex, is
questions.x: Ascon (e.g. Leucosolenia) has a single spongocoel lined by choanocytes; sycon (Scypha) has radial canals; leucon (Spongilla) has flagellated chambers and is the most complex.

questions.q: The coelom of echinoderms such as Asterias, which makes them deuterostomes like chordates, arises from
questions.x: Echinoderms are enterocoelous deuterostomes: the coelom buds off the archenteron and the blastopore becomes the anus. Annelids, arthropods and molluscs are schizocoelous.

questions.q: In birds, exchange of gases in the lungs takes place in the
questions.x: Air sacs act only as bellows that keep air flowing one way through the lungs; gases are exchanged in the air capillaries around the parabronchi. Birds have no alveoli.
questions.trap: Air sacs move and store air but have no gas exchange.

questions.q: The pecten, a comb-like vascular structure in the eye that nourishes the retina, is characteristic of
questions.x: The pecten projects from the retina into the vitreous humour of birds and supplies nutrients and oxygen to the retina.

questions.q: Moulting (ecdysis) in insects is mainly brought about by the hormone
questions.x: Ecdysone from the prothoracic glands starts each moult. Juvenile hormone only decides whether the moult gives another larva or the adult.
questions.trap: Juvenile hormone controls the type of moult, not the moult itself.

questions.q: The larva is bilaterally symmetrical but the adult becomes asymmetrical due to torsion in
questions.x: During development gastropods undergo torsion (180° twisting of the visceral mass), making the adult asymmetrical. Asterias adults are radially, not asymmetrically, built.

questions.q: Periodic reversal of the direction of blood flow, as the heart's peristaltic wave reverses, is seen in
questions.x: The tubular heart of the urochordate Herdmania pumps by peristalsis whose direction reverses every few minutes, so blood flow reverses too.

questions.q: Totipotent cells that bring about regeneration in flatworms such as Planaria are
questions.x: Neoblasts of Planaria can form any cell type. Archaeocytes are the totipotent cells of sponges, interstitial cells those of Hydra; flame cells are excretory.

questions.q: Electric organs that can give a strong electric shock are found in
questions.x: Torpedo has electric organs made of modified muscle that stun prey and enemies.

questions.q: A tetraneurous nervous system, with two pedal and two pleuro-visceral nerve cords, is found in primitive members of
questions.x: Primitive molluscs such as chitons have four longitudinal nerve cords (tetraneury). Annelids and arthropods have a ventral double nerve cord with ganglia; flatworms have a ladder-like system.

questions.q: Areolar connective tissue is found
o: In tendons, joining muscle to bone
In ligaments, joining bone to bone
Beneath the skin, joining it to the underlying muscles
questions.x: Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue that binds skin to muscles and surrounds vessels and nerves; tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue.

questions.q: The ectocervix (vaginal part of the cervix), from which a Pap smear is taken, is lined like the vagina by
questions.x: Moist surfaces facing wear (vagina, ectocervix, oesophagus, buccal cavity) have non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium; keratinised type is on skin.
questions.trap: Keratinised epithelium is only on dry skin surfaces.

questions.q: The follicles of the thyroid gland are lined by
questions.x: Cube-like cells of simple cuboidal epithelium line thyroid follicles, kidney tubules and small gland ducts, for secretion and absorption.

questions.q: Which of the following has the least capacity to regenerate in an adult?
questions.x: Mature neurons cannot divide, so lost neurons are not replaced. Liver, epidermis and bone repair readily.

questions.q: When the body wall of an earthworm is pricked with a needle, a milky fluid oozes out. This fluid is
questions.x: The coelom is filled with milky coelomic fluid, which also comes out through dorsal pores to keep the skin moist. The earthworm has closed circulation, so no haemolymph.

questions.q: In Pheretima, a pair of intestinal caeca arises from the intestine in segment
questions.x: The short conical intestinal caeca arise in segment 26 and extend forward to about segment 22; the typhlosole also begins in segment 26.

questions.q: The fold of mesentery that suspends the stomach of the frog is the
questions.x: Mesogaster holds the stomach; mesorchium holds the testes, mesovarium the ovaries and mesorectum the rectum.

questions.q: The end products of schizogony of Plasmodium, in human liver cells and red blood cells, are
questions.x: A schizont divides by multiple fission into many merozoites, which invade new RBCs. Sporozoites come from sporogony in the mosquito; the ookinete is the motile zygote.

questions.q: Chloragogen cells of the earthworm are functionally comparable to the vertebrate
questions.x: Chloragogen cells around the intestine store glycogen and fat, deaminate proteins to form ammonia and urea, and detoxify, like the liver.

questions.q: 'Two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely in the same place.' This statement is
questions.x: Gause showed with Paramecium species that the better competitor eliminates the other. Dollo: evolution does not reverse; Allen and Bergmann: body form and size vary with climate.

questions.q: Inside the human body, Plasmodium lives as an intracellular parasite in
o: White blood cells and lymph nodes
Liver cells and red blood cells
Nerve cells and the brain only
questions.x: Sporozoites first multiply in hepatocytes (exo-erythrocytic cycle); merozoites then enter RBCs (erythrocytic cycle).

questions.q: The sporozoite of Plasmodium is
questions.x: The sporozoite is a spindle- or sickle-shaped cell with one central nucleus and an apical complex; it moves by gliding.
questions.trap: The ring shape belongs to the early trophozoite in the RBC.

questions.q: The apical complex at the front end of sporozoites and merozoites of Plasmodium helps the parasite to
questions.x: Secretory organelles of the apical complex (rhoptries, micronemes) release substances that let the parasite enter liver cells and RBCs; it gives the phylum its name, Apicomplexa.

questions.q: Plasmodium is called digenetic because it
o: Completes its life cycle in two hosts, man and the female Anopheles
Has two nuclei in each cell
questions.x: Asexual schizogony occurs in man; gamete fusion and sporogony occur in the mosquito.

questions.q: Fusion of the gametes of Plasmodium in the mosquito's stomach is
o: Anisogamy, between a small microgamete and a large macrogamete
questions.x: The active microgamete (from exflagellation) fertilises the larger, passive macrogamete to form a zygote.

questions.q: In the life cycle of Plasmodium, the only diploid stage is the
questions.x: All stages in man and the gametes are haploid. The zygote and ookinete are diploid; meiosis in the young oocyst restores the haploid state.
questions.trap: Gametocytes make gametes but are themselves haploid.

questions.q: Plasmodium ovale causes
questions.x: P. ovale, like P. vivax, gives fever every 48 hours and can relapse from hypnozoites; it is milder than falciparum malaria.

questions.q: Cerebral malaria and blackwater fever are complications typical of infection by
questions.x: Falciparum-infected RBCs stick to small vessels (blocking brain capillaries) and massive haemolysis can turn the urine dark (blackwater fever).

questions.q: The antimalarial drug quinine is obtained from the bark of
questions.x: Quinine is an alkaloid from Cinchona bark. Artemisinin, another antimalarial, comes from Artemisia annua leaves.
questions.trap: Artemisia gives artemisinin, not quinine.

questions.q: In Pheretima, the fleshy lobe that overhangs the mouth on the first segment is the
questions.x: The first segment, peristomium, bears the mouth; the prostomium above it is a sensory lobe that also helps in burrowing.
questions.trap: Peristomium is the first segment itself, not the lobe above the mouth.

questions.q: The setae of the earthworm are
o: Glandular structures that secrete the cocoon
S-shaped chitinous bristles that help in locomotion
questions.x: Setae in each segment (except first, last and clitellum) grip the soil as circular and longitudinal muscles contract alternately.

questions.q: Dorsal pores of Pheretima begin from the intersegmental groove between segments
questions.x: Mid-dorsal pores are present from the 12/13 groove backwards; coelomic fluid comes out through them to keep the skin moist.

questions.q: Genital papillae of Pheretima are present on segments
questions.x: One pair of genital papillae lies on each of segments 17 and 19, near the male genital apertures on segment 18; they help in copulation.

questions.q: Earthworms are called 'friends of farmers' mainly because they
o: Burrow, loosen and aerate the soil and mix organic matter into it
questions.x: Burrowing improves drainage and aeration, and their castings return nutrients from deep soil, raising fertility.

questions.q: Vermicast is
o: Nutrient-rich castings (excreta) of earthworms used as manure
questions.x: Organic waste passed through the earthworm gut comes out as fine castings rich in N, P, K and microbes.

questions.q: Blood glands of Pheretima, which produce blood cells and haemoglobin, are present in segments
questions.x: Blood glands lie on the dorsal side of the pharynx in segments 4–6. Hearts are in 7, 9, 12 and 13; testes in 10 and 11.

questions.q: The single pair of ovaries of Pheretima lies in segment
questions.x: The ovaries hang from the septum between segments 12 and 13; oviducts open by the female pore on segment 14.
questions.trap: Segment 14 bears the female pore, not the ovaries.

questions.q: The skin of a frog stays moist and slimy because of secretions from its
questions.x: Mucous glands keep the skin moist for cutaneous respiration; frogs have no sweat glands and no scales.

questions.q: The numbers of digits on the forelimb and hindlimb of the frog are
questions.x: Forelimbs have four digits; hindlimbs have five webbed digits used for swimming and jumping.

questions.q: Frogs are poikilothermic, which means
o: Their body temperature changes with the temperature of the surroundings
They keep a constant body temperature
They have no blood vessels in the skin
questions.x: Cold-blooded frogs cannot regulate body temperature, so they hibernate in winter and aestivate in summer.

questions.q: In the frog, the eye is protected under water by the
questions.x: The thin, transparent nictitating membrane moves over the eye when the frog is in water. The tympanum is the eardrum behind the eye.

questions.q: In the frog, the arterial arch that supplies blood to the head is the
questions.x: The truncus arteriosus divides into carotid (head), systemic (body) and pulmocutaneous (lungs and skin) arches on each side.

questions.q: In the male frog, sperms reach the ureter after passing through the vasa efferentia and the
questions.x: Vasa efferentia from the testis enter the kidney and join Bidder's canal; from it sperms pass through uriniferous tubules to the ureter (urinogenital duct).

questions.q: In the frog brain, the paired optic lobes belong to the
questions.x: The midbrain has two optic lobes concerned with vision. The forebrain has olfactory lobes and cerebral hemispheres; the hindbrain has cerebellum and medulla.

questions.q: In the frog, the glottis opens into the
questions.x: The glottis on the floor of the buccal cavity leads into a short laryngo-tracheal chamber that opens into the two lungs.

questions.q: The skin of reptiles is
o: Dry, without glands, and covered with horny epidermal scales
questions.x: Keratinised scales and the lack of glands reduce water loss, letting reptiles live on dry land. Placoid scales belong to cartilaginous fishes.

questions.q: A wall lizard breaks off its tail when caught and later grows a new one. Shedding the tail in this way is
questions.x: Autotomy is self-amputation of a body part to escape a predator; the lost tail is regenerated. Ecdysis is moulting of the skin.

questions.q: Paired lateral flaps called parapodia, used for swimming, are found in
questions.x: Parapodia are characteristic of marine polychaetes like Nereis. Earthworms have only setae; leeches have neither.

questions.q: The excretory organs of annelids are
questions.x: Segmentally arranged nephridia remove wastes. Flame cells: flatworms; Malpighian tubules: insects; green glands: prawn.

questions.q: The non-cellular jelly-like layer between the outer and inner cell layers of Hydra is the
questions.x: Cnidarians are diploblastic: ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea in between, not a true germ layer.
questions.trap: Mesoderm is a true third germ layer, absent in Cnidaria.

questions.q: Coral reefs are built mainly from
o: The calcium carbonate skeletons of colonial coral polyps
questions.x: Coral polyps (class Anthozoa) secrete CaCO₃ skeletons that accumulate over thousands of years, e.g. the Great Barrier Reef.

questions.q: Ctenophores capture prey with special adhesive cells called
questions.x: Ctenophores lack cnidoblasts; sticky colloblasts on their tentacles trap small animals. Choanocytes belong to sponges.
questions.trap: Cnidoblasts belong to Cnidaria; ctenophores lack them.

questions.q: The short hollow outgrowth in the proboscis of Balanoglossus, once thought to be a notochord, is the
questions.x: Because the stomochord is not a true notochord, hemichordates are now usually placed among non-chordates.

questions.q: In urochordates such as Herdmania, the notochord is present
o: Throughout life, from head to tail
Only in the tail of the larva
In the head of the adult
questions.x: Hence the name Urochordata (uro = tail). The notochord is lost when the larva undergoes retrogressive metamorphosis.

questions.q: Which feature is ABSENT in cyclostomes such as Petromyzon?
questions.x: Cyclostomes are jawless vertebrates with a round sucking mouth, gill pouches and a persistent notochord, but no paired fins and no scales.

questions.q: Which pair of features belongs to a cartilaginous fish such as a shark?
o: A swim bladder and a terminal mouth
Ctenoid scales and a swim bladder
questions.x: Sharks have placoid scales, a ventral mouth, separate gill slits without an operculum and no swim bladder. Bony fishes have the other features.

questions.q: The heart of a fish
o: Has three chambers with mixed blood
Has two chambers and carries only deoxygenated blood
questions.x: One atrium and one ventricle pump venous blood to the gills; oxygenated blood goes from gills to the body without returning to the heart (single circulation).

questions.q: The lateral line system of fishes detects
questions.x: Neuromasts in the lateral line canal sense water movement and pressure changes, helping fish find prey and avoid obstacles.

questions.q: The voice box of birds, located where the trachea divides into bronchi, is the
questions.x: Birds produce sound in the syrinx; their larynx has no vocal cords. The pecten is in the eye; the crop stores food.
questions.trap: Larynx is the voice box of mammals, not birds.

questions.q: Two features found only in mammals are
questions.x: Hair on the skin and milk-producing mammary glands are unique to mammals. Birds and crocodiles also have four-chambered hearts.

questions.q: A smooth muscle fibre is
o: Spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus
questions.x: Smooth fibres are unstriated, involuntary and uninucleate. Multinucleate cylinders are skeletal fibres; intercalated discs are in cardiac muscle.

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of a myofibril, between two Z-lines, is the
questions.x: A sarcomere extends from one Z-line to the next; its shortening causes muscle contraction. Sarcolemma is the cell membrane of the fibre.

questions.q: The I-band of a skeletal muscle sarcomere contains
o: Both actin and myosin overlapping throughout
questions.x: The light I-band has actin only and is bisected by the Z-line; the dark A-band spans the whole length of the myosin filaments.

questions.q: Sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglion are
questions.x: A single process leaves the cell body and divides into a peripheral and a central branch. Bipolar neurons are in the retina; motor neurons are multipolar.

questions.q: The myelin sheath of nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord is formed by
questions.x: In the CNS, oligodendrocytes myelinate axons; Schwann cells do this only in peripheral nerves. Microglia are phagocytes; astrocytes support neurons.
questions.trap: Schwann cells form myelin only in the PNS.

questions.q: The yellow fibres of areolar connective tissue are made of the protein
questions.x: Yellow elastic fibres (elastin) are branched and stretchy; white fibres (collagen) are unbranched and tough.

questions.q: Bone cells that dissolve (resorb) bone matrix are
questions.x: Osteoblasts form new bone, osteocytes are mature cells in lacunae, and osteoclasts break bone down; together they remodel bone.
questions.trap: Osteoblasts build bone; they do not resorb it.

questions.q: The smooth articular surfaces at the ends of long bones in movable joints are covered by
questions.x: Glass-like hyaline cartilage reduces friction at joints. Elastic cartilage supports the pinna; fibrocartilage forms intervertebral discs.

questions.q: The simple squamous epithelium lining the inside of blood vessels and the heart is called
questions.x: Endothelium is a single layer of flat cells that lets materials pass easily. Mesothelium lines body cavities such as the pleura and peritoneum.

questions.q: The inner lining of the fallopian tube, which moves the ovum towards the uterus, is
questions.x: Beating cilia of the columnar cells, with muscular peristalsis, carry the ovum or embryo along the oviduct.

questions.q: Close similarity in the amino acid sequence of cytochrome c in humans and chimpanzees is an example of
questions.x: Similar molecules (proteins, DNA) in related species point to common ancestry; the more closely related, the fewer the differences.

questions.q: Thyroxine taken from a mammal can bring about metamorphosis in a frog tadpole. This supports
o: Common ancestry, shown by similar hormones in different vertebrates
questions.x: Hormones are chemically alike and act alike across vertebrates, a biochemical (physiological) evidence of evolution.

questions.q: The age of fossils is commonly found by
o: Radioactive (radiometric) dating, such as the carbon-14 method
Comparing body size with living animals
questions.x: Unstable isotopes decay at a fixed rate (half-life), so their ratio in a fossil or rock gives its age; C-14 suits remains up to about 50 000 years.

questions.q: Limulus (king crab) is called a 'living fossil' because it
o: Has remained almost unchanged for hundreds of millions of years
questions.x: Living fossils are present-day species closely resembling their ancient fossil ancestors, e.g. Limulus and Latimeria.
questions.trap: Peripatus, not Limulus, links annelids and arthropods.

questions.q: During development, the human heart passes through a two-chambered stage like that of a fish. This observation supports the
questions.x: Haeckel's law: ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny; embryos repeat stages resembling ancestral forms, such as fish-like heart and gill pouches.

questions.q: Lamarck explained the long neck of the giraffe by
o: Continuous stretching of the neck to reach leaves, passed on to the offspring
questions.x: Lamarck's use and disuse with inheritance of acquired characters. Darwin explained the same feature by natural selection of inborn variations.
questions.trap: Natural selection is Darwin's explanation, not Lamarck's.

questions.q: Lamarck put forward his theory of evolution in the book
o: Essay on the Principle of Population (1798)
questions.x: Origin of Species is Darwin's, Species Plantarum is Linnaeus's and the population essay is Malthus's.

questions.q: Balanoglossus is regarded as a connecting link between
questions.x: This hemichordate has pharyngeal gill slits and a hollow dorsal nerve cord (chordate-like) but a tornaria larva like that of echinoderms.

questions.q: J.B.S. Haldane described the primitive ocean, rich in organic molecules, as a
questions.x: Haldane proposed that UV light acting on the reducing atmosphere made organic molecules that collected in the sea, forming a hot dilute soup.

questions.q: The Miller–Urey experiment gave laboratory support to
o: Abiotic synthesis of organic molecules from simple gases (chemical evolution)
Origin of life from cosmic spores
questions.x: Amino acids formed from CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour with electric sparks, as the Oparin–Haldane theory had predicted.
